\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:responding}
\hlchaptermodality{3}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how someone is in Hindi, answer naturally, and return the question.}

Complete HI-C03-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: ask how someone is in Hindi, answer naturally, and return the question.

\section[kaise]{\hi{कैसे} (kaise) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} another of the k- questions}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-kaise}



\begin{quote}
You already met \hi{क्या} (\emph{kyā}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}). Here is its sibling — and, like all of Hindi's question-words, it starts with \textbf{k-}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\hi{क}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\hi{ै}} (the \emph{ai}-mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{कै}} (\emph{kai}); \textbf{\hi{स}} (\emph{sa}) + \textbf{\hi{े}} (the \emph{e}-mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{से}} (\emph{se}). Read \textbf{\hi{कै}·\hi{से}} $\to$ \emph{kaise}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{कैसे}} (\emph{kaise}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{कीदृश}} (\emph{kīdṛśa}, \textquotedblleft{}of what kind\textquotedblright{}) / the interrogative stem \textbf{\hi{क}-} (\emph{ka-}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the same question-root behind English \textbf{wh-} (what, who, how) and Latin \textbf{qu-}. Notice the pattern: Hindi's question-words are nearly all \textbf{k-} words — \emph{kyā} (what), \emph{kaun} (who), \emph{kab} (when), \emph{kahāṁ} (where), \emph{kaise} (how). Learn to hear the \emph{k-} and you can spot a question.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{कैसा} agrees}]
The adjective form \textbf{\hi{कैसा}} (\emph{kaisā}) changes to match what it describes: \emph{kaisā} (m.), \emph{kaisī} (f.), \emph{kaise} (m. plural / respectful). Because the respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} (\emph{āp}) takes a plural verb, \textquotedblleft{}how are \textbf{you}?\textquotedblright{} uses the plural \textbf{\hi{कैसे}} — that is the form you will use next.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{क} (\emph{ka}) + \hi{ै} (the \emph{ai}-mātrā) $\to$ \hi{कै} (\emph{kai}); \hi{स} (\emph{sa}) + \hi{े} (the \emph{e}-mātrā) $\to$ \hi{से} (\emph{se}). Read \hi{कै}·\hi{से} $\to$ \emph{kaise}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kaise\textquotedblright{}
  \item the k- question family — \emph{kyā, kaun, kab, kahāṁ, kaise}
  \item which English question-words share the root (what, who, how)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root do all of Hindi's question-words share, and what English family is it cousin to? (The interrogative \emph{k-}, PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}; the English \emph{wh-} words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}?]{\hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}? (āp kaise haiṁ?) — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-aap-kaise-hain}



\begin{quote}
Three words you already own, assembled into the first thing you ask after hello.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{हैं}} is \textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) + the \emph{anusvāra} dot \textbf{\hi{ं}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{हैं}} (\emph{haiṁ}), the nasalised plural. Everything else — \textbf{\hi{आप}} (\emph{āp}), \textbf{\hi{कैसे}} (\emph{kaise}) — you have met.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}?} = \textbf{\hi{आप}} (\emph{āp}, respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{कैसे}} (\emph{kaise}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{हैं}} (\emph{haiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you how are?}\textquotedblright{} Hindi keeps the verb \textbf{last}, exactly as in Chapter 2's \emph{merā nām … hai}. And because \emph{āp} is grammatically plural (that is how Hindi shows respect), its verb is the plural \textbf{haiṁ}, not the singular \emph{hai}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: respect is plural}]
To an elder or a stranger: \textbf{\hi{आप} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हैं}?} To a friend (\emph{tum}): \textbf{\hi{तुम} \hi{कैसे} \hi{हो}?} (\emph{tum kaise ho?} — \emph{ho} is the familiar \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{}). To no one in particular you would never drop to \emph{tū}. Match the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to the verb: \emph{āp … haiṁ}, \emph{tum … ho}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful question — \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?}
  \item the familiar version — \emph{tum kaise ho?}
  \item where the verb sits (at the end)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is it \emph{haiṁ} (plural) and not \emph{hai} with \emph{āp}? (Because respect in Hindi is grammatically plural — \emph{āp} always takes the plural verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maiṁ]{\hi{मैं} (maiṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} the m- of the first person}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-main}



\begin{quote}
To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} you first need \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} In Chapter 2 you learned \emph{merā} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}); here is its owner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{म}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\hi{ै}} (the \emph{ai}-mātrā) + the \emph{anusvāra} nasal \textbf{\hi{ं}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{मैं}} (\emph{maiṁ}). One nasal syllable.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मैं}} (\emph{maiṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{मया}} (\emph{mayā}, \textquotedblleft{}by me\textquotedblright{}), on the first-person root \textbf{\hi{म}-} (\emph{ma-}) — the same root that gave you \emph{merā} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) last chapter, and the same \textbf{m-} behind English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine} and Latin \emph{mē}. Hindi's \textquotedblleft{}I,\textquotedblright{} its \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} and English's \textquotedblleft{}me/my\textquotedblright{} all grow from one ancient first-person sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pronoun you can often drop}]
Hindi verbs carry the person in their ending, so \emph{maiṁ} is frequently left out once context is clear — much like Spanish or Latin. You will still learn it first, because the answer to \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?} begins with it: \emph{maiṁ …}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{म} (\emph{ma}) + \hi{ै} (\emph{ai}) + the \emph{anusvāra} \hi{ं} $\to$ \hi{मैं} (\emph{maiṃ}). One nasal syllable.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maiṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the m- family — \emph{maiṁ} (I), \emph{merā} (my), English \emph{me}, \emph{my}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root links \emph{maiṁ}, \emph{merā}, and English \emph{me}? (The first-person \textbf{m-}, from Sanskrit \emph{ma-} / PIE \emph{*me-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hūṁ]{\hi{हूँ} (hūṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}am,\textquotedblright{} cousin of English \emph{am}}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-hun}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 2 gave you \emph{hai} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}). This is the same verb in the first person — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I} am.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{ह}} (\emph{ha}) + \textbf{\hi{ू}} (the long-\emph{u} mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{हू}} (\emph{hū}); the \emph{chandrabindu} \textbf{\hi{ँ}} nasalises it $\to$ \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} (\emph{hūṁ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{हूँ}} (\emph{hūṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{अस्मि}} (\emph{asmi}, \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}) — the first-person of the very root that gave you \emph{hai}. That root, PIE \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}, is the \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} of the whole family: Sanskrit \emph{asmi} $\to$ English \textbf{am}, Latin \emph{sum}, Greek \emph{eimi}; Sanskrit \emph{asti} $\to$ \emph{hai} / English \emph{is}. So the Hindi copula lines up with English person by person: \textbf{\hi{हूँ}} \emph{am}, \textbf{\hi{है}} \emph{is}, \textbf{\hi{हैं}} \emph{are}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} table so far}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
I & \emph{maiṁ hūṁ} & I am \\
you (resp.) & \emph{āp haiṁ} & you are \\
he/she/it & \emph{vah hai} & he/she is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The verb \textbf{\hi{होना}} (\emph{honā}, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}) is the frame every sentence hangs on; you now have three of its faces.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{ह} (\emph{ha}) + \hi{ू} (long \emph{u}) $\to$ \hi{हू} (\emph{hū}); the \emph{chandrabindu} \hi{ँ} nasalises $\to$ \hi{हूँ} (\emph{hūṃ}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hūṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the copula trio — \emph{hūṁ} (am), \emph{hai} (is), \emph{haiṁ} (are)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maiṁ … hūṁ\textquotedblright{} — I am …
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit word is \emph{hūṁ} from, and its English cousin? (\emph{Asmi}, \textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}; English \textbf{am} — same PIE root \emph{*h\textsubscript{1}es-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{ठीक}]{\hi{ठीक} (ṭhīk) — \textquotedblleft{}fine,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-thik}



\begin{quote}
The word that answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and does a dozen other jobs besides.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\hi{ठ}} (\emph{ṭha}, a \textbf{retroflex} \emph{th} — tongue curled back to the roof of the mouth) + \textbf{\hi{ी}} (the long-\emph{ī} mātrā) + \textbf{\hi{क}} (\emph{ka}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{ठीक}} (\emph{ṭhīk}). The retroflex \hi{ट}-\hi{ठ}-\hi{ड} series is a hallmark of Indian languages; the tongue touches further back than for an English \textquotedblleft{}t.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{ठीक}} (\emph{ṭhīk}) means \textquotedblleft{}correct, right, fine, exactly, OK.\textquotedblright{} It is a genuinely \textbf{native} Indian word — no European cousin to hand — and one of the most useful in the language: \emph{ṭhīk hai} (\textquotedblleft{}OK / agreed\textquotedblright{}), \emph{ṭhīk samay} (\textquotedblleft{}the right time\textquotedblright{}), \emph{sab ṭhīk?} (\textquotedblleft{}all well?\textquotedblright{}). Not every word has a far-flung cognate, and that is worth seeing too: \emph{ṭhīk} is Indian to the core.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{The exchange — the reply}
Put it together with Chapter 3's atoms: \textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{ठीक} \hi{हूँ}} (\emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am fine}.\textquotedblright{} Literally \textquotedblleft{}I fine am,\textquotedblright{} verb last. Add thanks: \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād.} And the whole exchange stands:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?} (\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād.} (\textquotedblleft{}I'm fine, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{ठ} (\emph{ṭha}, a \textbf{retroflex} \emph{th} — tongue curled to the roof of the mouth) + \hi{ी} (long \emph{=\textbackslash{}i}) + \hi{क} (\emph{ka}) $\to$ \hi{ठीक}. The retroflex \hi{ट}-\hi{ठ}-\hi{ड} series is a hallmark of Indian sound.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ṭhīk\textquotedblright{} — feel the retroflex \emph{ṭh}
  \item the full reply — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ}
  \item the casual \textquotedblleft{}OK\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ṭhīk hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the whole reply to \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?}, and say what is special about \emph{ṭhīk}'s origin. (\emph{Maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ}; it is a native Indian word with no European cognate.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{आपका} \hi{स्वागत} \hi{है}]{\hi{आपका} \hi{स्वागत} \hi{है} (āpkā svāgat hai) — \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-aapka-swagat-hai}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you, this is what you say back — and it hides a word Sanskrit uses whole, unchanged.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
The key word is \textbf{\hi{स्वागत}} (\emph{svāgat}): the conjunct \textbf{\hi{स्व}} (\textbf{\hi{स्}} \emph{s} + \textbf{\hi{व}} \emph{va} $\to$ \emph{sva}) + \textbf{\hi{ग}} (\emph{ga}) + \textbf{\hi{त}} (\emph{ta}). Add \textbf{\hi{आपका}} (\emph{āpkā}, \textquotedblleft{}your,\textquotedblright{} from Chapter 2) and \textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{स्वागत} \hi{है}} = \textquotedblleft{}your welcome is\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you are welcome}.\textquotedblright{} The heart of it, \textbf{\hi{स्वागत}} (\emph{svāgat}, \textquotedblleft{}welcome\textquotedblright{}), is Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{सु}} (\emph{su-}, \textquotedblleft{}well, good\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{आगत}} (\emph{āgata}, \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{well come},\textquotedblright{} exactly like English \emph{welcome}. Two deep roots hide inside:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{su-} \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} is the twin of Greek \textbf{eu-} (\emph{euphoria}, \emph{eulogy}).
  \item \emph{āgata} is from the root \textbf{\hi{गम्}} (\emph{gam}, \textquotedblleft{}to go/come\textquotedblright{}), cousin of English \textbf{come}.
\end{itemize}

Sanskrit's own \emph{svāgatam} is this very word, unchanged — here it is again, worn into everyday Hindi.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
The key word \hi{स्वागत} (\emph{svāgat}): the conjunct \hi{स्व} (\hi{स्} \emph{s} + \hi{व} \emph{va} $\to$ \emph{sva}) + \hi{ग} (\emph{ga}) + \hi{त} (\emph{ta}), with \hi{आपका} (\emph{āpkā}, “your”) and \hi{है} (\emph{hai}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āpkā svāgat hai\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \emph{svāgat} is built from (\emph{su} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āgata} \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{})
  \item the exchange — \emph{dhanyavād} / \emph{āpkā svāgat hai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{svāgat} literally mean, and what English word matches it piece for piece? (\textquotedblleft{}Well come\textquotedblright{}; English \textbf{welcome}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 3 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:HI-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, assembled from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (respectful) — \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm fine, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}You're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{āpkā svāgat hai.}
  \item the familiar version of the question — \emph{tum kaise ho?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the k- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kaise})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{} (\emph{maiṁ}, \emph{hūṁ})
  \item the copula trio you now hold (\emph{hūṁ / hai / haiṁ})
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kaise} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{k-} (PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}), cousin of English \emph{how/what}
  \item \emph{maiṁ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ma-} (PIE \emph{*me-}), cousin of English \emph{me/my}
  \item \emph{hūṁ} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{asmi}, cousin of English \textbf{am}
  \item \emph{svāgat} $\leftarrow$ \emph{su} + \emph{āgata} = \textquotedblleft{}well come,\textquotedblright{} matching English \textbf{welcome}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
A stranger asks \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?} — give a complete, polite reply, then thank-and-welcome the exchange back. (\emph{Maiṁ ṭhīk hūṁ, dhanyavād.} — and if thanked, \emph{āpkā svāgat hai.})
\end{tcolorbox}
